variants.name: Validating constructor on an opaque type
variants.idiom_name: pub fn new(...) -> Result<Self, E> / TryFrom on a type with private fields
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's visibility rules already forbid the failure mode the Essence guards against: a struct with private (non-pub) fields cannot be built with a `Contract { .. }` literal outside its module, so a `pub fn new(...) -> Result<Self, ContractError>` that validates every compulsory property before the value is formed IS the Essence, and the module system replaces the friend/package-private restricted constructor. Validation runs before the value exists, so there is no half-constructed object to leak and no exception path - failure is an ordinary `Result` value (`TryFrom`/`FromStr` are the standard spellings for fallible conversions; `From` stays reserved for infallible ones). The classic two-class Essence is still justified when many compulsory properties would make `new` unwieldy or when clients fill in properties incrementally across an API boundary: a builder whose `build(self)` performs the cross-field checks keeps the same always-valid guarantee, and a staged/typestate builder moves it to compile time.
pitfalls: A `pub` field, `impl Default`, or a stray tuple constructor forges a path around validation: `Default::default()` yields an instance that violates the invariants by definition, so an Essence-guaranteed type keeps every field private and does not derive `Default`.

Implementing `From<T>` (or any check-free constructor) for inputs that can be invalid hands callers a silently-invalid or panicking path; `From` promises an infallible conversion, so use `TryFrom`, `FromStr`, or a `Result`-returning `new` and report which compulsory property failed.

Derived `serde::Deserialize` constructs the struct field-by-field without running `new`, so a wire format or config file can mint invalid instances - parse at the boundary into the validated type (custom `Deserialize` or `try_from` after deserializing the draft).
Panicking constructors (`expect`/`unwrap` inside `new`) turn ordinary user input into process aborts; reserve panics for programmer bugs and return `Result` for recoverable validation failures.

Creation-time validation pins the invariant only at t0: any `&mut self` setter can invalidate the object afterwards, so keep Essence-guaranteed types immutable and make changes go through a validating constructor again.

variants.name: Staged/typestate essence: incomplete property lists are compile errors
variants.idiom_name: consumed-self staged builder with PhantomData markers; finish() only on the complete state
variants.implementation_notes: The runtime Essence becomes a type-level protocol: `Essence<C, S>` is parameterized by zero-sized markers (`Missing`/`Given`) carried in `PhantomData<(C, S)>`, and each staged setter consumes `self` and returns the type with one marker advanced, so `finish(self) -> Contract` is only ever defined on `Essence<Given, Given>` - skipping a compulsory property is a compile error, not a runtime `Err`, which is the staged-builder route the record's own use cases name. Zero-sized markers make the staging free at run time and the consumed `self` prevents reusing a spent essence. Worth the extra types when the Essence is a public boundary that untrusted callers program against; inside one crate the plain `Result`-returning `new` is simpler and just as safe.
pitfalls: A transition that takes `&mut self` cannot swap the `PhantomData` marker type, so a builder that mutates in place silently stops enforcing completeness - every staged setter must consume `self` and return the advanced type.

The marker type participates in variance and auto-trait inference through `PhantomData<(C, S)>`; a staged essence that must be `Send`/`Sync` needs markers preserving those properties (`PhantomData<fn() -> S>` if in doubt).
The enforcement lives in the type system, so nothing checks completeness at run time: mark staged setters `#[must_use]` so a dropped half-built essence warns instead of vanishing silently.
